profile.reading:
Sabey Data Centers operates SDC Seattle, a two-part data center campus in Tukwila, King County, Washington, marketed by the operator as the West Coast's largest privately owned data center campus. Sabey traces its roots to 1972, when Dave Sabey founded Sabey Corporation as a Pacific Northwest commercial real estate developer; the company entered the data center business almost by accident during the dot-com collapse, when a vacated tenant building in this same Tukwila location became SDC Seattle Building 5, prompting Sabey's pivot into the data center industry. Sabey Data Centers itself was formally established in 2010 as a joint venture between Sabey Corporation and institutional investor National Real Estate Advisors, a structure confirmed on both the operator's own site and independently by Wikipedia. As of 2026 Sabey operates seven data center campuses nationally, together totaling more than 3.5 million square feet and, per Wikipedia's most recent figure, nearly 400 MW of capacity; Tim Mirick became Sabey's president effective January 1, 2025, succeeding Rob Rockwood.

Per the operator's own SDC Seattle page, the Tukwila campus totals more than a million square feet and 54 MW of capacity campus-wide, a figure not broken out per individual building and not applied to any single structure here. Aggregator sourcing indicates the campus actually comprises two separately addressed sub-campuses: Intergate.East, at a street range of 3311 to 3511 South 120th Place, Tukwila, WA 98168, spanning roughly 1.2 million square feet; and Intergate.West, at 12101 to 12301 Tukwila International Boulevard, Tukwila, WA 98168, built in 1999 and spanning roughly 173,000 square feet.

This building, Intergate.West Building B, is listed by aggregator Datacenters.com at 12201 Tukwila International Boulevard, Tukwila, WA 98168, a specific number falling within the campus-wide range described by other aggregator sources and between neighboring Buildings C (12101) and A (unconfirmed, campus range applied).
profile.capacity_note: not published at the building level. Campus wide total is 54 MW (operator figure) across the Tukwila campus, not applied to this individual building.
profile.research_note: Gap-view review: Sabey publishes SDC Seattle only as a campus-wide total (1M+ sqft / 54MW across Intergate.East + Intergate.West sub-campuses), not broken out per building. No per-building figure exists for Intergate.West Building B. No numeric key written.

reading.body:
Sabey Data Centers operates this facility as part of a larger Tukwila campus without publishing power capacity at the individual building level, making its direct contribution to regional AI infrastructure opaque from public sources.

The Intergate Seattle West sub-campus, built in 1999 and spanning roughly 173,000 square feet, is one of two physically separate data center complexes within what operators market as a single Seattle location. The broader Tukwila campus totals 54 megawatts of capacity across multiple buildings, but Sabey does not allocate this power to specific buildings in public disclosures. This opacity is common practice among operators who prefer to market capacity at the campus level rather than expose individual facility utilization or remaining availability.

Sabey's national footprint now spans Washington, Virginia, New York, Texas, and Oregon, with recent growth into the Austin metro region and planned expansion in Oregon. The company's Pacific Northwest campuses, including this one, rely partly on hydroelectric power, which differs materially from the grid dependencies that constrain AI infrastructure in most other regions. This registry tracks only the Washington state facilities, meaning the majority of Sabey's capacity growth lies outside the scope of what this page can show about regional compute concentration.

Without building-level power disclosures, assessing how much capacity supports AI workloads versus other data center tenants remains impossible from available sources. The research status is complete, but completeness here means documenting what is and is not knowable rather than filling gaps with estimates.
